Your AI agent decides what to do. MELRA governs how tool calls are authorized, verified, and recovered.
An open-source local execution runtime for agent tool calls you route through MELRA.
It checks each call against policy, requests approval when needed, verifies declared
evidence, and keeps a redacted receipt of what runs to an outcome. For each task, MELRA
dispatches mutations at most once; uncertain outcomes are parked for reconciliation
instead of replay. Exactly-once external effects still depend on the provider. Calls
made through other tools remain outside MELRA's control.

In a terminal,

...

Write it into ~/project/.mcp.json? [Y/n]
✓  Workspace    ~/project
✓  Policy       ~/.melra/policy.json
✓  Claude Code  ~/project/.mcp.json
Next: Start claude in this workspace and approve the 'melra' server when it asks; 'claude mcp list' then shows it connected.
Then restart your agent app (Claude Code asks you to approve a project's server
once) and ask it to do something, for example

show me the system info"

What is MELRA?
AI agents no longer just talk. They edit files, run commands, click through websites
and call APIs on your behalf. Four questions come with that, and most agents answer
them differently, or not at all:
🛡️ Is it allowed?
Every action MELRA receives is checked against
your
policy, and checked again at
the moment it runs. Risky changes wait for your exact approval.
✅ Did it really work?
"No error" is not success. An action counts only when the
evidence you declared
holds: the file exists, the exit code is 0, the page says what it should.
🔁 What if it crashes?
Every mutation MELRA dispatches is
recorded before it runs
and runs
at most
once
. After a crash, MELRA settles it from its evidence or the provider; what it
cannot settle waits in
recovery_required
and is never replayed.
🧾 What happened?
Every action MELRA runs to an outcome leaves a
redacted, hash-linked receipt
, so
you can audit what ran, who asked, and why it was allowed.
MELRA answers those questions in one place for tool calls routed through it, across
supported agents. It sits underneath your agent for those calls, the way an operating
system sits underneath your apps:
The LLM reasons. The harness manages the loop. MELRA governs the effect lifecycle
for calls routed through it.
Swap the model or the agent; MELRA's policies,
approvals, credentials, history and receipts can stay in place.
Works with your agent
MELRA speaks the
Model Context Protocol
, so any MCP
client can use it. For these,
melra setup --client <name>
writes the config in the
client's own format and location, and
melra doctor
tells you whether each one is

or the

A named client is marked

How it works
An
effect
is one bounded operation an agent routes through MELRA:
file.write
,
terminal.run
,
browser.click
,
http.request
, and so on. MELRA handles each routed
effect in nine stages, split between a plan step and an execute step (for a single
task,
melra_plan
then
melra_execute
) so that
nothing runs at planning time
:
Here is one change from start to finish, in developer mode. In
enforced mode
the challenge carries no
phrase: you approve with
melra approve <task-id>
outside the conversation,
and the agent's
melra_execute
sends no approval at all.
sequenceDiagram
autonumber
participant A as Your agent
participant M as MELRA
participant You
participant W as Your system
A->>M: melra_plan: write notes.md, evidence "file contains 'done'"
M->>M: type, classify, check policy, record
M-->>A: awaiting_approval + challenge "APPROVE 3f9c…"
A->>You: May I write notes.md?
You-->>A: yes
A->>M: melra_execute with the exact phrase
M->>M: policy again, not already done?
M->>W: write the file (under a budget)
M->>W: read it back, independently
M-->>A: verified_success + receipt

, and what an agent should do next:
Status
Meaning
Next step
🟢

Done
🟡

Look at the evidence, then decide
🔴

Read the reason; the same request will be refused again
🔵

A change is waiting for your approval
Developer mode: approve it from the agent that planned it. Enforced mode:
melra approve <task-id>
⏳

semantic

Nothing can answer it yet; it settles closed at expiry
🟣

The task reaches
verified_success
only if the process exits
0
. A process that runs
and exits
1
completed the action but failed the evidence, so it is reported as
partial
. MELRA never receives a goal like
"fix the production server"
: that needs
judgement, which belongs to the model. A kernel that interpreted sentences would be a
kernel whose guarantees depended on a model.
When an agent connects, MELRA also sends it a short guide to this loop (the MCP
server's
instructions
), so a model knows to declare evidence, read the status, and
never blindly retry an unknown outcome, without anyone prompt-engineering it.
See what it is doing
You can see each action MELRA handled and its policy decision, and, for each that ran
to an outcome, its evidence and receipt, from the terminal or the browser. Nothing here
can approve or start work, and approval phrases are never displayed.
From the terminal
$ melra status
MELRA 0.3.0-alpha.17  developer mode
Tasks       3 total: 1 awaiting_approval,
1 policy_blocked, 1 verified_success
Waiting     1 waiting for approval
HTTP        127.0.0.1:7457 not running
$ melra tasks
ID        STATUS             OPERATION     UPDATED
64199678  awaiting_approval  file.write    0s ago
ca4aec7a  policy_blocked     terminal.run  1s ago
a1285e0f  verified_success   system.info   1s ago
$ melra watch          # live, until Ctrl-C
6:07:21 PM  task 882cf55c  verified_success
6:07:22 PM  task f813364c  awaiting_approval
melra doctor
checks Node, SQLite, the browser and policy, and reports which of your
agent apps point at MELRA, with the one command that fixes anything wrong.
In the browser:
melra serve --http --open
An overview, a searchable task list, and durable workflows with a live event stream.
It works at phone width and in light and dark, and it is served with a strict
Content-Security-Policy.
Safe by default
Default
🏠
Local only.
stdio, loopback HTTP behind a token, or a mode-
0600
Unix socket only your OS user can open. No account and no hosted service.
📴
Telemetry is off.
✍️
Changes need two things:
declared evidence
and
an exact, expiring, task-scoped approval: a phrase in developer mode, an operator's
melra approve
in enforced mode.
📁
Paths stay inside your workspace
, including terminal working directories; symlink escapes are refused.
🚫
Shells,
sudo
/
su
and arbitrary desktop key names are denied.
Terminal commands must be on the allowlist by name.
🌐
Private, link-local and cloud-metadata addresses are blocked
by the browser and HTTP adapters themselves, after DNS resolution, before any allowlist is consulted; loopback too in enforced mode, unless the policy opens it.
⚠️
Web page content is marked untrusted
and can never change policy.
🔑
Secrets are redacted
before anything is stored, and agents get capabilities, never your raw credentials.
⏱️
Every call is bounded
by a budget and a cancel signal; a stalled browser fails with a clear error instead of hanging.
Unsafe-local mode and the two deployment modes
Every row above can be switched off at once with
melra serve --unsafe-local
(or
MELRA_UNHINGED=1
): no policy, no approvals, no evidence requirement, no workspace
confinement, no destination checks. The agent gets exactly the reach your OS user has.
The mode announces itself on stderr, in
melra doctor
and in
melra_capabilities
,
and receipts still record what ran. See
unsafe-local mode
.
The honest gap in a default install is that MELRA governs the effects it is
asked
for
. An agent holding both a MELRA terminal and a native one makes the kernel
optional.
MELRA_MODE
is where you say which situation you are in:
Mode
Meaning
developer
(default)
MELRA governs what it is asked for; the agent may have another path, and you accept that. This is why MELRA can be tried in thirty seconds.
enforced
You assert the alternative is gone: the agent is sandboxed, holds no privileged secrets, and reaches these systems only through here.
MELRA cannot verify that assertion from inside its own process, and it does not
pretend to; the isolation is the operating system's job. What enforced mode does is
close every door MELRA owns:
--unsafe-local
is refused outright, nothing binds
outside loopback (a
0600
Unix socket is allowed), no client can register itself, and
mode
is stamped on every receipt. For the operating-system side,
examples/deploy
has a hardened Docker run and systemd
unit, each checked in CI, and
melra doctor
reports which restrictions are actually in
effect. See
deployment modes
,
the
threat model
and the
security policy
.
Why MELRA
An LLM decides
what
to do. A harness runs the loop that gets it there. Something
still has to decide whether the resulting effect is allowed, avoid replaying uncertain
mutations, prove what happened, and survive a crash in the middle. Today that machinery
is rebuilt inside every agent harness, and it dies with the harness. MELRA is that machinery,
factored out and made agent-independent.

Plenty of MCP servers

The difference is that in MELRA they are the execution contract rather than a per-tool
option. The boundary is
partly shipped

MELRA owns, but the OS isolation that stops a harness reaching the filesystem
around

#52

The feature test.
Anything that would still make sense if the request came from
ordinary deterministic software belongs in MELRA: authorisation, idempotency,
credential isolation, recovery, verification, effect history. Prompt optimisation, LLM
memory, model selection, a planner and agent personality belong to the harness above.
That is why nothing in MELRA's execution path ever calls a model.
What it can do
Effect adapters
The kernel is the contract; these are its shipped implementations. Every one passes
through the same policy, approval, budget, verification, receipt and certificate
pipeline; an adapter that skipped it would not be an adapter.
Adapter
What is implemented
🗂️
Files
Root-confined read, hash, atomic write, move, mkdir and delete, with symlink-escape defenses
💻
Terminal
Shell-free foreground and supervised background processes with allowlists, traits, timeouts, interactive input, cancellation and redaction
🌐
Browser
Isolated Playwright sessions, semantic DOM targets, bounded artifacts, network and popup policy, opt-in profiles, condition-based settling, and every browser call bounded so a stalled page fails clearly
🖥️
Computer
Capability discovery, accessibility-tree and OCR inspection, and governed screenshot, pointer, drag, keyboard and scroll on macOS, Windows and supported Linux/X11 setups
📡
HTTP
GET
/
HEAD
as reads and every other method as an approval-gated at-most-once mutation, pinned to the address the destination check resolved, with credentials injected by the kernel rather than handed to the caller
🧠
Operational memory
A kernel service, not an adapter: scoped SQLite storage of what MELRA knows about its own effects, with hybrid ranking, freshness, expiry, supersession, provenance and redaction
Database, cloud and SaaS adapters are designed and on the
roadmap
, not
shipped today. Semantic memory about the
user
(preferences, conversation history)
belongs to the harness, not here.
A deliberately small tool surface
Eleven tools in front of the adapters and one durable workflow controller. The CLI,
both SDKs, loopback HTTP and the Unix socket reach the same eleven operations; this
list is the kernel contract, not an MCP-specific API.
Tool
Purpose
melra_capabilities
Discover operations, platform support, limits and policy posture
melra_plan
Validate, persist and policy-check one bounded operation
melra_execute
Execute an approved plan and verify the declared outcome
melra_task_status
Read durable task state
melra_task_cancel
Cooperatively cancel pending or running work
melra_receipt
Retrieve redacted evidence and the execution certificate
melra_workflow_plan
Validate, preflight, encrypt and persist a bounded workflow
melra_workflow_advance
Execute one ready scheduling wave
melra_workflow_status
Read the durable workflow projection
melra_workflow_cancel
Cooperatively cancel nonterminal workflow work
melra_workflow_control
Pause, resume or suspend a run without losing its place
Prefer tool names your model already knows? Set
MELRA_HARNESS_TOOLS=1
and thirteen
more appear alongside these (
read_file
,
write_file
,
run_command
,
browser_click
,
approve
, …). They are not a second path: each one builds an ordinary task and runs
the same pipeline. See
ordinary tool names

Durable, restart-safe workflows
Workflows compose
operation
,
approval
,
condition
,
parallel
,
bounded_loop
,
checkpoint
,
compensation
,
human_input
and
delegation
nodes, and every effect
still travels through the task pipeline. Each CLI call below is a new process, so this
exercises restart persistence with no daemon:
melra workflow plan --definition examples/workflows/restart-safe.json
#
save the id
melra workflow advance
<
workflow-id
>
melra workflow advance
<
workflow-id
>

#
developer mode echoes the phrase; enforced mode runs `melra approve <task-id>` instead

<
workflow-id

--approval
'
<approval-id>:<exact phrase>
'

<
workflow-id

planned            stateVersion=2
running            stateVersion=4   inspect=verified_complete

running            stateVersion=10  write=verified_complete

Stop the process after any line and the next command resumes from the same
MELRA_HOME

repeated. They are settled by re-observation, or they park in
recovery_required
